title: Threat Actors and Motivations: The Official Matrix

blocks.text: Objective **2.2** expects a classification: **who attacks, why, and with what means**. The four provided books discuss actors and intelligence, but do not give the full matrix required by the exam objectives: it is therefore written here from the official objectives and flagged as such.

blocks.note: Official objectives — none of the 4 books provides the full actors × motivations matrix

blocks.field: Individual or group conducting malicious activity. The objectives distinguish eight categories, classified notably by motivation, resources, and level of sophistication.

Typical Profile

rows: Structured groups, often with a business model and professional tools

blocks.text: This matrix of eight actors and their motivations is **required in §2.2** of the SY0-801 objectives, but none of the four books presents it in this form. The examples above are educational applications of the objectives, not quotes from a book.

blocks.note: Actors, attribution, and threat intelligence (printed pp. 161-167) — partial source, not the official taxonomy

items: **Financial motivation**: monetary gain, fraud, selling stolen data.
**Influence**: shaping an opinion or behavior.
**Intellectual property**: theft of trade secrets or research.
**Notoriety**: gaining fame, claiming credit for an exploit.
**Espionage**: gathering information for a state or employer.
**Fear / chaos**: causing panic or paralysis.
**Extortion**: ransom, blackmail, threat of disclosure.
**General curiosity**: exploring without financial motive.
**Revenge**: retaliation against an employer or third party.
**Ideological motivation**: acting for a belief or movement.
**Political motivation**: serving a political or electoral goal.
**Ethical motivation**: "testing" or exposing without authorization — a motive often claimed by hacktivists.

blocks.text: Motivation is the most reliable **classification criterion**: the same tool (ransomware) can be financial for organized crime or ideological for a hacktivist. The tool does not define the actor.

The SOC notes and the Defensive Security Handbook provide useful landmarks — external attacker, insider threat, targeted campaigns — but they do not replace the official categories. Remember the **actor ↔ motivation** pairing rather than group names, which are explicitly excluded from the exam.

blocks.q: A disgruntled employee exfiltrates customer data to harm their employer. Which actor ↔ motivation pairing is correct?
blocks.explain: Legitimate access qualifies the actor as an insider; revenge is the described motivation.

items: Eight actors: organized crime, terrorist, unskilled, hacktivist, insider, accidental, competitor, state-sponsored.
Twelve motivations, from money to ethics, including ideology and revenge.
Motivation classifies the actor, not the tool used.
Official matrix = §2.2 objectives, absent from the four books.

blocks.text: Identifying an actor is not limited to their name: the exam expects you to reason about **three attributes** — internal or external position, financial resources, and level of sophistication — and then about the **confidence** you can place in an attribution.

blocks.field: An internal actor has legitimate access to the environment; an external actor must first cross the boundary. The insider is the most dangerous case because they bypass perimeter controls.
Financial and material capacity of the actor: it governs campaign duration, purchasing of tools or vulnerabilities, and use of third parties.
From using off-the-shelf scripts to developing custom tools and exploiting zero-days. An APT stands out through persistence and adaptation.

items.title: 1. Observe Techniques
items.text: Observed tactics and techniques (phishing, lateral movement, exfiltration) rather than a single IOC.

items.title: 2. Evaluate Attributes
items.text: Internal or external, resources, sophistication: three axes of characterization.

items.title: 3. Compare Against Motivations
items.text: The targeted objective (money, espionage, ideology) points to the actor category.

items.title: 4. Attribute Cautiously
items.text: Express a confidence level and update the profile when new evidence arrives.

blocks.text: Trap: attributing an actor based on a single IP address or a single tool. Tools are shared and infrastructure can be rented. The exam favors a **body of evidence** and a coherent motivation.

blocks.note: Investigation stories: profiling without absolute certainty

blocks.q: Which element best distinguishes a state-sponsored actor from an unskilled attacker?
options: The level of sophistication and resources committed over a long campaign
The presence of a phishing email
blocks.explain: Attributes (resources and sophistication) distinguish a backed APT from an opportunist using off-the-shelf scripts.

items: Three attributes: internal/external, resources/funding, sophistication.
An insider already has legitimate access: perimeter controls do not block them.
Attribution relies on a body of evidence and is expressed as a confidence level.
The full taxonomy is provided by the §2.2 objectives, not by the books.
